thread.document:
For any question that depended on my own training runs / plots / metrics, I explicitly asked it to: State what it couldn’t know, and then ell me what I needed to fill in from my own notebook (accuracy numbers, screenshots, etc.).

For pure theory/math derivations (e.g., rewriting softmax with a Gaussian kernel, deriving the linear attention complexity, causal recurrences), the LLM: Got the structure right on the first try.

For high-level conceptual questions (example difficulty, why early exit helps, what hooks do, when to use early exit vs a smaller model): It also mostly one-shotted reasonable, coherent answers. I’d estimate ~70–80% of the non-coding questions were basically “done” after a single pass, with only minor wording tweaks from me.

A few consistent failure modes showed up: Over-confidence on unknown experiment outputs, Numeric details from papers , Flattening subtle distinctions

Here are the strategies that seemed to work best to keep the LLM honest:

Ask for derivations, not just final answers

Force it to separate “what it knows” from “what I must provide”

Compare against the original paper

Ask for structure, then fill in details myself
